downloads.title: Our data
downloads.description:
Chile's Millennium Nucleus on the Impacts of China in Latin America and the Caribbean (ICLAC), the Inter-American Dialogue, and our partners are pleased to make our Chinese foreign direct investment data available to researchers and other users of the Repository.

The full dataset —every investment across all countries in a single file— is available for download below. As we add new countries, they will be incorporated into the same dataset.

We welcome you to submit contributions or corrections through the Contact page. We are grateful for your help keeping our data as accurate and up to date as possible.

map.title: About the map
map.body:
The Regional Repository maps Chinese foreign direct investment (FDI) and construction projects across Latin America, classified by type, sector, and company.
On the map, points are single-site investments (mines, plants, offices) and vectors mark projects spanning several cities (roads, railways, cables). The toggle groups by country into pie charts and switches between number of projects and amount. The book icon means the investment has an academic case study.

sankey.title: About the diagram
sankey.body:
The diagram shows the Investor → Country → Sector flow of Chinese FDI, over the same data as the map.
Each flow's width reflects the chosen metric: number of investments or amount (US$ MM). Investors are grouped by canonical company (top 20; the rest roll up into "Others"). Click any node to filter by it. Country, sector, and year filters are shared with the map.

methodology.title: Methodology
methodology.description:
The Regional Repository of Chinese Investments in Latin America represents a collective endeavor to map Chinese foreign direct investment (FDI) and construction projects in the Latin American region between 2003 and 2025, and to classify these investments by project type, economic sector, and companies involved. At present, the Repository contains data for Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, Ecuador, Paraguay, Peru, and Uruguay.


How was the Repository developed?


The production of this Repository is a collaborative endeavor, involving researchers and research institutions from across the Americas. Our team is composed of researchers with wide-ranging, interdisciplinary backgrounds, including political scientists, economists, and geographers. Our work is also made possible by the dedicated participation of numerous research assistants and undergraduate and graduate student researchers from the many universities and research centers affiliated with this project. We are grateful for the contributions of Eugenio Sánchez from Sciences Po; Florencia Muñoz, Gonzalo Concha, Benjamín Muñoz, Catalina Leiva, and Allison Stronach from the Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile; and Yifang Wang and Xinyi Wang from the Inter-American Dialogue. Additionally, we acknowledge the extensive contributions to our research from Juliana González Jauregui in Argentina and Darissa Cama in Peru. When compiling our Peru data, we were fortunate to partner closely with the Center for China and Asia-Pacific Studies (CECHAP) at the Universidad del Pacífico. We aim to expand to incorporate more countries in close collaboration with other regional partners.


The Repository was produced by assembling data from ICLAC and partner data sets on Chinese foreign direct investments (FDI) in specific Latin American countries, according to the OECD definition of FDI, which assumes a long-term relationship between the direct investor and the direct investment company or asset and a significant degree of influence (at least 10 percent ownership) over the management of the company. Under «construction» we have also included projects that have been built by Chinese companies but wherein the companies retain no ownership. We analyzed each project using primary and secondary sources to confirm the amount, purpose, location (including geocoordinates), and local partners for each investment in our data set. Our methodology for project selection concluded with an extensive peer review process involving in-country partners and other experts.


What does the Repository include?


Our map visualizes China's investments using both points and vectors, to better represent each project's geographical ambit. We have used points for investments in assets, such as mines, real estate, or agricultural sites, that don't traverse multiple cities. Vectors are utilized for roads, rail, cables, and oil blocks. All aim to provide an accurate representation of the extent of Chinese engagement on a country-by-country and sectoral basis. There is one instance in Chile in which a Chinese company, Tianqi Lithium, acquired a minority stake in a local conglomerate—SQM—which owns many, varied assets across the country. In this instance, we have not visualized all of SQM's assets in the Repository, but rather those related to lithium, which were the primary motivation for Tianqi Lithium's acquisition. This is an effort to avoid visually overrepresenting Tianqi Lithium's 25 percent participation in SQM. In each instance, we have aimed to achieve a balance between precision and clarity in the visualization.


The map offers a relatively simplified representation of project locations. However, by downloading the data, users can determine the city or locality where Chinese investments are located, along with other details about each transaction. Our data is accessible in a CSV format by clicking on the Download Data tab at the top of the page.


We have additionally incorporated high-quality, peer-reviewed case study analysis of these projects, when available, to assist researchers as they pursue new avenues of inquiry or fill critical research gaps. This includes analysis from peer-reviewed journal articles, doctoral dissertations, think tank reports, or government documents that thoroughly examine one or more investments in the Repository. Featured studies contain at least one page of analysis on the China-related project or investor and were published since China invested in or financed the project in question. As users will observe, the research gaps on Chinese investment in these countries are substantial. Only a small percentage of the total projects have affiliated case studies, which we indicate with a book icon.


The Repository includes greenfield investments, mergers and acquisitions, and joint ventures, all of which feature in our data and are classified accordingly. It is also limited to projects that are currently operational. For instance, if assets were once owned by a Chinese company but later sold, they are not included in our data. Projects that have been announced but for which there is no financing, or sign of «lasting interest» or «significant degree of influence,» have also been excluded from our data. Numerous projects that have been covered extensively in the media have been excluded from the Repository because no progress is evident to date, or else finance has yet to materialize. At the same time, if mining concessions are purchased but remain undeveloped, we have included these deals in the dataset, because they reflect «lasting interest» in mining assets, unless the concession has expired or is suspended. When projects contain both the acquisition of an initial asset and then greenfield investment in that same asset (e.g., an expansion of an existing dam), these projects are classified as acquisitions.


All of the projects in the Repository are classified by industry. For our purposes, the infrastructure classification comprises all transport and facilities-related (e.g., hospitals) investments, including turnkey construction projects. Energy investments include oil and gas, hydroelectricity projects, and renewable energy investments. Investments in banking or insurance are classified as Finance, but the purchases of office space by Chinese banks that are establishing themselves in the region are labeled as Real Estate transactions. The same is true of other warehouse or office purchases, including by Chinese tech conglomerates. Agrobusiness incorporates any agricultural investments, including food-related deals and agrochemical investments. Thus far, our manufacturing category includes only machinery, car, and bus manufacturing. The projects categorized as Mining each include the acquisition or development of mining sites, but also any possible related investment in mining equipment, investments related to site preparation, site-specific infrastructure, exploration, and other related activities.


In addition to foreign direct investment, the Repository also attempts to capture instances of Chinese construction, often through public works contracts, which have historically been an important feature of Chinese infrastructure engagement with the Latin American region. In these cases, Chinese companies retain no ownership of these assets. Their obligations cease once construction is finished.


Can Repository users contribute information on Chinese investments in Latin America?


As noted, all Repository data is the product of a rigorous research process that has included the triangulation of primary and secondary data sources, as well as consultations with experts to verify the details of documented transactions. However, we are aware that the landscape of FDI in the region is continually evolving. We appreciate your collaboration in keeping our data as accurate and up to date as possible. We invite users to contribute to and edit our data via the «Contact Us» tab located at the top of our page.


The Repository is made possible with funding from Chile's Nucleo Milenio program, which promotes collaborative research in support of Chile's development, and by the Henry Luce Foundation. We hope that the data will be used to advance academic research and other analysis.


Suggested citation: Francisco Urdinez and Margaret Myers (2025) «Regional Repository of Chinese Investments in Latin America,» ICLAC and Inter-American Dialogue.
